context.text: An investor is comparing four regional engineering consultancies.

context.title: Last year

prompt: Which firm has the highest revenue per employee?
solution: Revenue per employee: Brightwell $150k, Corvane $180k, Delmont $140k, Estova $190k
shortcut: Divide millions by thousands and you get thousands: 95 ÷ 0.5 = 190. The biggest firm is not the most productive.

context.text: A private school has 1,260 pupils and 84 teachers. Its board wants no more than 14 pupils per teacher, with the same number of pupils.

prompt: How many extra teachers must the school hire?
shortcut: Today's ratio is 1,260 ÷ 84 = 15; at 14 the school needs 1,260 ÷ 14 = 90 teachers.

context.text: An online homeware shop compares last month's marketing channels.

context.title: Marketing channels, last month

prompt: Which channel had the lowest marketing cost per purchase?
solution: Cost per purchase: search $30, social $25, email $22.50, display $40
shortcut: Divide spend by purchases and ignore clicks; display ads have the cheapest clicks but the dearest purchases.

context.text: Country X has a GDP of $1.8 trillion and a population of 60 million. Country Y has a GDP of $450 billion and a population of 25 million.

prompt: Country X's GDP per person is approximately how many times Country Y's?
shortcut: Ratio of GDPs (4) divided by ratio of populations (2.4): 4 ÷ 2.4 ≈ 1.67.

context.text: A logistics company is funded by $36m of debt and $54m of shareholders' equity.

prompt: What percentage of its total capital is debt?
shortcut: Debt to total capital, not debt to equity: 36 ÷ 54 = 67% is the trap.

context.text: Last week Plant A made 5,400 units with 18 workers over a 6-day week. Plant B made 4,200 units with 12 workers over a 5-day week.

prompt: By what percentage is Plant B's output per worker per day higher than Plant A's?
shortcut: Divide by workers and days. Per worker alone (300 against 350) gives 17%, the trap.

context.text: A property developer is ranking four refurbishment projects by annual return on the money invested.

context.title: Refurbishment projects

prompt: Which project offers the highest annual return on investment?
shortcut: Put both in thousands and compare ratios; the biggest profit (Cedar) has the lowest return.

context.text: A paint maker measures its relative market share: its own sales divided by the sales of the market leader. In a $2.4bn market it sells $360m, against the leader's $600m. Next year it expects its sales to grow by 25%, the leader's by 5% and the market by 10%.

prompt: What will the paint maker's relative market share be next year?
shortcut: Relative share ignores the market size: 0.6 × 1.25 ÷ 1.05 = 0.75 ÷ 1.05 ≈ 0.71.

context.text: A sports retailer had annual revenue of $110m and cost of goods sold of $73m. It held $12m of inventory, valued at cost, on average through the year.

prompt: How many days of inventory does the retailer hold, measured against cost of goods sold?
shortcut: 73 ÷ 365 = 0.2 exactly. Inventory is held at cost, so measuring it against revenue (40 days) is the trap.

context.text: A regional health network compares nurse staffing at its four hospitals.

context.title: Hospital staffing

prompt: Which hospital has the most nurses per occupied bed?
solution: Occupied beds: Ashgrove 180, Bellmead 190, Carrow 200, Dunholm 135
shortcut: Per bed, Dunholm leads (2.07), but per occupied bed Ashgrove's empty wards lift its ratio to 2.5.

context.text: A fashion chain operates three store formats.

context.title: Average store by format

context.text: The chain is considering converting its outlet sites to the street-store format, using the same floor space.

prompt: If an outlet site's space then matched street-store sales per square metre, by what percentage would sales on that site rise?
shortcut: Compare sales densities only; the number of stores the site holds does not matter.

context.text: A wildlife charity raised $4.2m last year. It spent $3.6m: $2.7m on programmes, $0.6m on fundraising and $0.3m on administration.

prompt: How much did the charity spend on fundraising for each dollar it raised?
shortcut: Per dollar raised, so divide by what came in ($4.2m), not by what was spent ($3.6m gives $0.17).

context.text: A warehouse operator is comparing two automation options.

context.title: Automation options

prompt: The operator will choose automated storage only if its annual return on investment is at least as high as the sorting robots'. What is the most it should invest in automated storage?
solution: Sorting robots: ($45k − $12k) × 12 = $396k a year on $1.5m, a return of 26.4%
shortcut: Equal returns means investment in proportion to net savings: $1.5m × 40 ÷ 33 ≈ $1.82m. Ignoring running costs gives $1.5m × 60 ÷ 45 = $2.00m, the trap.

context.text: An e-commerce company runs four fulfilment warehouses and wants to know which is the cheapest per order shipped.

context.title: Monthly warehouse data

prompt: Which warehouse has the lowest staff and rent cost per order shipped?
shortcut: Staff cost per order alone favours West ($3.77); adding rent per order ($1.50 at South, $1.90 at West) flips the ranking.

context.text: Plant A runs three 8-hour shifts a day, each staffed by 30 workers, and produces 450 tonnes of animal feed a day. Plant B runs one 10-hour shift a day, six days a week, staffed by 25 workers, and produces 2,100 tonnes a week.

prompt: Plant B's output per worker-hour is how many times Plant A's?
solution: Plant A: 30 × 3 × 8 = 720 worker-hours a day; 450 ÷ 720 = 0.625 tonnes per worker-hour
Plant B: 25 × 10 × 6 = 1,500 worker-hours a week; 2,100 ÷ 1,500 = 1.4 tonnes per worker-hour
shortcut: Put both on worker-hours before comparing. Forgetting Plant A's three shifts gives 0.75.

context.text: A furniture maker has a current ratio (current assets ÷ current liabilities) of 1.6, with current liabilities of $25m. It uses $5m of cash, a current asset, to pay off $5m of current liabilities.

prompt: What is its current ratio after the payment?
shortcut: Taking the same amount off both sides of a ratio above 1 pushes it up. Reducing only the assets gives 1.40, the trap.

context.text: A swimmer goes to the pool 3 times a week, except for 4 weeks of holiday a year, when she does not go at all. Any membership must be paid for the whole year (52 weeks).

items: Plan A: $45 a month, unlimited visits
Plan B: $380 a year plus $2 per visit
Plan C: pay as you go at $10 per visit
Plan D: $30 a month plus $1.50 per visit

prompt: Which plan gives her the lowest cost per visit?
solution: Per visit: A $3.75, B ≈ $4.64, C $10, D $4.00; lowest: Plan A
shortcut: With visits fixed, the cheapest plan per visit is just the cheapest plan per year; Plan B's low headline fee loses once visit charges are added.

context.text: An insurer's call centre handles 18,000 calls a week, each lasting 6 minutes on average. Agents work 37.5 hours a week and spend 75% of that time on calls; the rest goes on training and admin.

prompt: How many agents does the call centre need?
solution: Call time: 18,000 × 6 minutes = 108,000 minutes = 1,800 hours a week
shortcut: 1,800 ÷ 37.5 = 48 agents at full utilisation, then ÷ 0.75 = 64.

context.text: Nutrela, a packaged-food company, earns nearly all its revenue in mature economies and now wants to build a business in faster-growing ones.
The board's main worry is entry risk: how unpredictable demand will be in a new country. A common guide to this is how sharply the country's GDP growth has swung from one year to another.

context.title: Table 2: Data on the four countries being considered
rows: Highest GDP growth in any one year, last 5 years
Lowest GDP growth in any one year, last 5 years
Credit risk grade (A: highest to E: lowest)
Bribery perception score (1: cleanest to 10: worst)

prompt: Which of the following lists is the best ranking of R, S, T and V on entry risk, from the LEAST risky to the most risky?
solution: Swings in growth are best measured by highest minus lowest growth.
Least to most risky: T, R, S, V.
shortcut: S and V clearly have the widest gaps, with V far ahead, so only T against R needs a subtraction.

context.text: Solmar runs beach resort hotels in two countries and is choosing a third destination for its next resort.
Demand risk is the uncertainty about how many visitors a destination will attract in future, which is often indicated by how much the destination's tourist arrivals rise or fall from year to year.

context.title: Table 3: Shortlisted destinations

prompt: Which of the following lists is the best ranking of destinations W, X, Y and Z in terms of demand risk, from the LEAST risky to the most risky?
solution: How much arrivals swing is best measured by highest minus lowest growth.
Least to most risky: Y, X, Z, W.
shortcut: W and Z obviously swing the most, W by far, which leaves a quick Y against X subtraction.

context.text: Calcora produces cement and has plants in three countries. It wants to build a fourth plant in a fast-growing market.
Market risk describes how uncertain the future size of a country's building market is; it is often indicated by how much the country's construction output growth varies from year to year.

rows: Highest yearly growth in construction output (best of the last 5 years)
Lowest yearly growth in construction output (worst of the last 5 years)

prompt: Which of the following lists is the best ranking of the countries (F, G, H, J) by market risk, from the LEAST risky to the MOST risky?
solution: Variation in growth is best measured by highest minus lowest growth.
Least to most risky: G, H, J, F.
shortcut: F and J are the only countries with a year of falling output, so they are the two riskiest, F clearly more; G against H is one quick subtraction.

prompt: Suppose Dishdash will go ahead with live order tracking only if its annual return on investment is higher than that of faster delivery. Which of the following statements is accurate?
options: The company would be prepared to invest a maximum of $45m upfront in live order tracking
The company would be prepared to invest a minimum of $45m upfront in live order tracking
Live order tracking would need to deliver a return on investment of at least 20%
Live order tracking would need to deliver a return on investment of at most 20%
solution: That return is the hurdle live order tracking has to clear, so the true statement is that it requires at least 20% (C); at most 20% (D) has the comparison backwards
Live order tracking's annual profit = 11,000 × 365 × $3.30 − 12 × $0.37m = $8.81m, so the most the company could invest and still match 21% is $8.81m ÷ 0.207 = about $43m, which rules out A and B
shortcut: Faster delivery: 12,000 × $3 is $36k a day, about $13m a year; less about $4m of monthly costs leaves $9m on $45m, about 20%. That is the hurdle, so tracking requires at least 20%; its $8.8m a year at 21% supports only about $43m up front.
